section_summary: This section follows American and Allied discussions of Japan’s proposed postwar constitution from November 1945 through June 1946. It includes criticism of the existing imperial system, reports on successive drafts, the revised Japanese and English texts, and debate over how to ensure that adoption reflects the Japanese people’s free will. The final pages begin a policy study on the respective authority of the Far Eastern Commission and General MacArthur.

subfiles.title: Atcheson to Acheson on constitutional revision
subfiles.about: Atcheson urges a public American statement before Konoe’s committee publishes an imperial-sanctioned draft.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson fears Konoe’s committee will preserve imperial power and impede democratic government. He reports MacArthur’s instruction not to discuss its draft, encloses a proposed press statement, and urges the State Department to release it promptly.

subfiles.title: Draft statement to the press on the Japanese Constitution
subfiles.about: The proposed statement sets out democratic standards for constitutional reform in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Citing the Potsdam Declaration and American policy, the draft argues that Japan must choose its own constitutional form while removing obstacles to democracy. It criticizes executive and imperial power, the House of Peers, Privy Council, military autonomy, limits on rights, and state-sponsored religion. It calls for representative legislative control, a responsible cabinet, equal participation, and protection of fundamental rights.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Chinese Embassy on constitutional reform
subfiles.about: Penfield briefs Tsui on American contacts with Japanese constitutional reformers.
subfiles.summary: Penfield says no known British or American technicians are drafting with the Japanese and working-level talks have been suspended.

subfiles.title: Japanese press report on Cabinet constitutional revisions
subfiles.about: Atcheson reports the Cabinet committee’s expected changes to the Meiji Constitution.
subfiles.summary: Press accounts predict reduced imperial prerogatives, stronger popular rights and Diet powers, and changes to military, treaty, budget, peerage, judicial, and Privy Council provisions, while retaining the first four articles.

subfiles.title: Hindustan Standard editorial on the new Japanese Constitution
subfiles.about: A Calcutta editorial criticizes the American influence visible in Japan’s proposed constitution.
subfiles.summary: The report summarizes an editorial portraying the draft as American-written and criticizing U.S. policy in Japan.

subfiles.title: Johnson forwards Thompson’s constitutional suggestions
subfiles.about: Johnson passes along a letter that McCoy thought relevant to the constitutional study.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Thompson’s letter for possible use in studying the Japanese Constitution.

subfiles.title: Thompson to McCoy on enforcing renunciation of war
subfiles.about: Thompson proposes criminal sanctions and international trials for violations of Japan’s proposed ban on war.
subfiles.summary: Thompson argues that constitutional renunciation of war needs penalties for individuals and enforceable trial procedures. He suggests an international court, invokes the weakness of the Kellogg-Briand Pact, and cites Walter Lippmann’s ideas on sanctions.

subfiles.title: Matsumoto requests Japanese draft constitution
subfiles.about: Matsumoto seeks a copy of the revised constitution, especially its civil rights provisions.
subfiles.summary: Requests the draft’s civil rights provisions and asks about an opportunity to visit Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Matsumoto on constitution availability
subfiles.from: Acting Chief, Japan and Korea Branch
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Matsumoto’s request for the constitution.
subfiles.summary: Says copies are unavailable for distribution but encloses a broadcast version of the civil rights section.

subfiles.title: Copy of Matsumoto’s request to Bowles
subfiles.about: A typed copy repeats Matsumoto’s request for the constitutional text.
subfiles.summary: Copy of Matsumoto’s request to study civil rights provisions and hear of possible travel to Japan.

subfiles.title: Revised Draft of Japanese Constitution
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Atcheson transmits revised Japanese and English newspaper texts and identifies substantive amendments.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports the government’s colloquial-language revision of April 17 and lists changes concerning imperial diplomatic functions, emergency Diet sessions, secret meetings, selection of the prime minister, judicial retirement, and transitional provisions. It notes favorable reaction to the simpler language alongside criticism of the draft’s structure.

subfiles.title: Revised Japanese draft constitution
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Japanese-language reproduction of the revised constitutional draft.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese text, heavily degraded in OCR, contains draft articles on war renunciation, rights, government, amendment, and transitional provisions.

subfiles.title: Revised English draft constitution
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: English-language reproduction of the revised constitutional draft.
subfiles.summary: The text sets out popular sovereignty, the emperor’s limited functions, renunciation of war, rights and duties, the Diet, cabinet, judiciary, finance, local autonomy, amendment, and supremacy provisions. Supplementary articles govern implementation and transition from the existing constitutional order.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Commission discussion of SWNCC 228/2
subfiles.about: Borton reports disagreement over criteria and procedures for adopting the new constitution.
subfiles.summary: Committee 3 deletes proposed language on adoption machinery and considers whether the present Diet should have final approval. Borton recommends supporting a New Zealand proposal or, failing that, election of a new Diet for final approval.

subfiles.title: Appendix to SWNCC 228/2 on adoption machinery
subfiles.about: The appendix proposes principles and possible procedures for adopting a new constitution.
subfiles.summary: Calls for full discussion, legal continuity, and demonstrated popular consent, with hearings, elections, or a referendum as possible methods.

subfiles.title: Hilldring submits proposed telegram to MacArthur
subfiles.about: Hilldring asks urgent consideration of a proposed message to MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: Requests committee review of the attached proposed telegram.

subfiles.title: Proposed telegram to MacArthur on FEC liaison
subfiles.about: The draft urges MacArthur to send a trusted officer to consult with the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledging MacArthur’s staffing concerns, the draft argues that direct discussion in Washington could reduce disputes over constitutional reform and the respective responsibilities of SCAP and the Commission.

subfiles.title: Hilldring submits revision to SWNCC 228/2
subfiles.about: Hilldring requests consideration of an attached revision to the adoption criteria.
subfiles.summary: Forwards proposed wording for SWNCC 228/2.

subfiles.title: Proposed revision to SWNCC 228/2
subfiles.about: The revision addresses alternative means of adopting Japan’s constitution.
subfiles.summary: Proposes allowing a constituent assembly, specially elected Diet, or popular referendum if the Japanese people desire one.

subfiles.title: FEC action on criteria for constitutional adoption
subfiles.about: Borton reports the Commission’s adoption of general criteria and continued dispute over detailed procedures.
subfiles.summary: The FEC adopts the first paragraph of the criteria while referring contested language on alternatives to the present Diet back to committee.

subfiles.title: Draft FEC criteria for adopting a new constitution
subfiles.about: The attached draft elaborates criteria for popular approval of the constitution.
subfiles.summary: Its surviving text calls for legal continuity and questions whether the present Diet alone may consider or adopt the constitution.

subfiles.title: Vincent forwards Far Eastern policy papers
subfiles.about: Vincent sends papers on Japan’s constitution, Korea, and reparations for possible discussions in Paris.
subfiles.summary: Notes that SWNCC has not acted on the constitutional paper and that the reparations proposals lack a formal State Department position.

subfiles.title: SWNCC 228/3 circulation note
subfiles.from: Alexander D. Reid, B. L. Austin, and Harold W. Moseley
subfiles.about: The secretariat circulates a State Department study for committee consideration.
subfiles.summary: Circulates the State member’s study on adoption of a new Japanese constitution.

subfiles.title: United States policy on adopting a new Japanese constitution
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends policy statements and a message to MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: Recommends approval of appended policy statements and transmission of guidance to MacArthur and the U.S. FEC representative.

subfiles.title: Facts bearing on constitutional adoption
subfiles.about: Appendix A traces statements and decisions concerning the proposed constitution.
subfiles.summary: It recounts MacArthur’s March announcement, Byrnes’s remarks, the FEC’s March directive, MacArthur’s April address and May objections, and the FEC’s May adoption criteria. The chronology highlights disagreement about Allied review, Japanese public discussion, and the Commission’s authority.

subfiles.title: Discussion of FEC and SCAP positions
subfiles.about: Appendix B compares positions on constitutional adoption and Allied review.
subfiles.summary: The analysis contrasts FEC concern for ample debate and review before Diet approval with SCAP’s preference for speed, Diet adoption, and limited Commission intervention. It describes the U.S. position as seeking cooperation with the Commission while preserving MacArthur’s authority, and recommends formal policy guidance.

subfiles.title: Proposed statement on the FEC’s function in passing on the constitution
subfiles.to: United States representative on the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Appendix C defines the Commission’s proposed authority to assess the final constitutional draft.
subfiles.summary: The statement says Japan may adopt a constitution under its own procedures if it meets surrender terms and the Potsdam Declaration. It limits FEC review to consistency with controlling requirements, rejects routine formal approval of each provision, and favors review just before the Diet’s final vote.
